title: Cognitive Biases
description: Systematic patterns in how people judge and decide.

options: Favoring information that supports existing beliefs
Overestimating how much others notice you
Judging a decision by its outcome alone
Relying on the first number you hear
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is the tendency to seek, interpret and remember evidence in ways that confirm what we already believe.

questions.prompt: Which of these are cognitive biases or heuristics?
questions.explanation: Anchoring, the availability heuristic and the sunk cost fallacy all describe distortions in judgment. Classical conditioning is a learning process, not a judgment bias.

questions.prompt: After seeing several news reports about plane crashes, a person rates flying as more dangerous than driving. Which mechanism is most likely at work?
questions.explanation: Vivid, easily recalled examples make an event feel more frequent than it is, even though driving is statistically far riskier per mile.

questions.prompt: Under the sunk cost fallacy, people keep investing in something because of what they have already spent, even when future costs outweigh future benefits.
questions.explanation: Past, unrecoverable costs should not affect a forward-looking decision, but they often do.
